newsitem.title: UK: Mark unfazed by German data, Irish punt steadies.
newsitem.headline: Mark unfazed by German data, Irish punt steadies.

text.p: The mark was steady against most European currencies, unfazed by a slower-than-expected German M3 growth in April and a jump in the Ifo economic research institute's business climate index.

Traders were watching the Irish punt, which rebounded from the three-week low it set against the mark Wednesday amid concern it will have to fall to its central rate in Europe's exchange-rate mechanism before the launch of economic and monetary union.

German M3 money supply grew 6.7 percent on an annualised basis in April from the fourth quarter of 1996, closer to the Bundesbank's 4.5-6.5 percent target range than the 8.3 percent growth rate seen in March.

The report didn't ignite any hopes of lower German rates, though, as the Ifo institute reported an increase in its business climate index to 94.7 in April from 92.6 in March. Also, Bundesbank council member Olaf Sievert said he saw no need to change German rates at the moment.
There was some interest in the punt following its near-2-percent plunge against the mark yesterday.

Traders focused on a Goldman Sachs report which said it will either have to fall towards its ERM parity rate of 2.4111 marks or be revalued if central ERM parities are used as the conversion rates between the currencies of countries joining European economic and monetary union.

"There is a good chance that the idea of using central parities rates as a conversion rate will be adopted as it creates the least political problems," said Guenter Thumann, EMU advisor at Salomon Brothers in London.
"Since the Irish punt is still well above its parity, market participants have been making money out of betting that it will need to come down by quite a bit."

The punt fell as low as 2.5535 marks before rebounding to 2.5734/64 from 2.5643/58 Wednesday. It was trading 6.15 percent stronger than its central ERM parity rate against the mark. The Irish currency hasn't traded at its central ERM parity rate against the mark since September 9, 1996.
The mark held gains it made against the Swiss franc after the Swiss National Bank added liquidity to the money markets for the second day running in a bid to prevent the franc from strengthening.

"The SNB doesn't really want the franc much below 84 and will continue to make its point by adding liquidity until the market gets it," said Robin Poynder, the chief foreign exchange dealer at Charterhouse Bank.
The mark was last at 83.30/32 centimes, from 83.26/28 late Wednesday.

The mark was confined within its recent ranges against the Italian lira, with traders expecting a cut in the Bank of Italy's discount rate after preliminary consumer price data from 11 Italian cities released yesterday and Tuesday suggested the inflation rate will fall to 1.5/1.6 percent in May.
Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi added to such expectations after he said conditions were in place for a rate cut. Mark/lira was last at 985.10/50 from 984.35/75 Wednesday.
